d.title: You are billed for the thinking you never see
d.caption: Reasoning tokens are output tokens: they are generated, billed and then discarded before the response reaches you. On the worked example — 500 reasoning plus 50 visible — **90.9% of what you paid for is invisible**. The bottom rows are why this needs a budget rather than a default: a 200-token answer at the quoted 100× reasoning ratio is 20,200 billed tokens, forty times the cost of the same answer from a non-reasoning model.

d.title: reasoning_effort is choosing how much search to pay for
d.caption: The parameter is not a quality dial. It buys **search over approaches**, so it is worth paying for only when there is a search to do. The first row is the one that saves the most money: extraction, classification and formatting have no search in them at all, and a cheap non-reasoning model is both faster and orders of magnitude cheaper. The last row is the one that surprises people — thinking time is wall-clock time, and a 10,000-token trace is seconds of silence.

d.title: Raise on the empty case rather than returning nothing
d.caption: A reasoning model can spend its whole budget thinking and return **no visible text at all** — a successful response, billed in full, with an empty content field. The temptation is to return `""` and let the caller decide, but that pushes an invisible failure into code with no way to recognise it, and the symptom surfaces much later as a blank field in a UI or a record with a missing summary. Raise, and let the retry logic see it.

d.title: Detail is a 9x price dial, and often buys nothing
d.caption: One 1024×1024 image costs $0.001912 at `detail=high` and $0.000212 at `low` — **9.0×**, measured. Whether that is worth paying turns entirely on whether the question needs resolution. "Is there a person in this photo?" is answered by a 512-pixel view, and nine times the tokens changes nothing. "What does this sign say?" is exactly what the tiles are for.

d.title: Image tokens are input tokens, and they cannot be truncated
d.caption: Everything from 1.5 applies unchanged — image tokens count against the window and leave less room for output. What is different is that they arrive in **large indivisible blocks**. You can drop a retrieved chunk to make room; you cannot shave 200 tokens off an image. So a multimodal budget has to be computed before the prompt is assembled, not trimmed afterwards.

nodes.label: So text cannot be trimmed to fit
nodes.sub: the block is all or nothing

nodes.label: Or decide to send fewer images

d.title: Plausible-but-wrong costs more to find than obviously-wrong
d.caption: A vision model will read a scanned document, often well. It will also cost 765 tokens a page at high detail, take seconds, and occasionally hallucinate a digit — and that is the whole argument. **An OCR engine with low confidence produces garbage that is obviously garbage**; a vision model produces plausible numbers. The first failure is caught by the next person who looks; the second is caught by an audit, months later, if at all.

d.title: What a stream hands you, chunk by chunk
d.caption: A stream is a sequence of deltas, and the fields you need are not all in the same place. Content arrives in `delta.content`, which is **absent on some chunks** rather than empty. `finish_reason` arrives on the final chunk, so the truncation check of 1.5 happens at the end, not the start. And usage arrives last of all, or only if you asked for it — so a cost counter that reads it eagerly reads nothing.

nodes.label: finish_reason on the last chunk
nodes.sub: so check truncation at the end

nodes.label: usage last, or only on request

d.title: HTTP 200 arrives before the answer does
d.caption: A non-streaming request either succeeds or fails, and you find out before you have anything. A stream returns **200 as soon as the first chunk is ready** — so an error at token 400 arrives *after* you have already shown the user 399 tokens. There is no status code left to send, which means the handling cannot be an exception path: the UI has to be able to retract or mark a partial answer, and that is a design decision rather than a `try` block.

d.title: Streaming costs the same, unless you abandon it
d.caption: Same tokens, same price — streaming is not a discount. The exception is that a stream can be **abandoned**: stop reading, close the connection, and the server stops generating, so tokens never produced are never billed. Three situations make that worth building, and the first is simply common: in a chat UI people navigate away from long answers all the time, and closing the stream on unmount is a small change with a real saving.

d.title: Half price, for agreeing to wait
d.caption: The batch API trades latency for 50% off, and the question it asks is only whether anything is waiting. The three yes rows are **free money** — the work is offline and deadline-free, so the discount costs nothing. The last row is the one to think about rather than answer quickly: a submitted batch is committed work, so a pipeline that might need to cancel mid-run is a poor fit even when nobody is waiting.

d.title: The cache matches a prefix, so one variable token at the front costs everything
d.caption: Prompt caching keys on the **longest common prefix**, which makes message order a pricing decision. Static system text and documents first, variable user content last, and the cache hits. Put the query first and one variable token invalidates every static token behind it — measured on this workload, **$125.00 per 100,000 requests** for an ordering that looks like a style preference.

nodes.label: Nothing behind it can match
nodes.sub: one token invalidates all of it

d.title: The tokeniser is part of the price
d.caption: Two encodings over the same six samples disagree on exactly one of them — and it is the one that matters internationally. The same French text is **73 tokens in cl100k and 57 in o200k**, a 22% difference with no change to the text at all. English prose, code and UUIDs come out within a token either way. So a cost model built by measuring English and applied to a multilingual product is wrong in a direction that depends on the language.

nodes.label: So measure in your own encoding

d.title: The chat envelope nobody counts
d.caption: Messages are not just their content. Each one carries about 3 tokens of structural overhead and the reply is primed with 3 more — which on a short conversation is **9 tokens of envelope on 13 of content, a 69% overhead**. It stops being alarming at scale: on a 50-turn conversation of 20-token messages the envelope is 153 of 1,153 tokens, about 13%. The lesson is that short-message workloads pay a tax that long-message ones do not.

d.title: A price table, and a claim it does not support
d.caption: The same call priced four ways spans a factor of 66, from $0.000450 to $0.030000 — which is the real argument for routing rather than picking one model. The second half is a correction worth carrying: **GPT-4o-mini is widely called "30× cheaper" than GPT-4o, and its own price table says 16.7×** on both input and output. Still an enormous saving, and not the number people repeat.

d.title: Three places to call the counter
d.caption: A token counter is only useful where it changes a decision. Call it **before sending** to enforce the budget of 1.5; in an **admission check** to reject a request that cannot possibly fit, rather than discovering it from a 400; and in **logging**, so every request carries its own estimated cost and the bill is reconcilable without waiting for an invoice. Reconcile `PER_MESSAGE` and `PER_REPLY` against a real `usage.prompt_tokens` once, then trust it.

d.title: The five differences that are not cosmetic
d.caption: Most of the support matrix is noise — a missing `top_k` on OpenAI is harmless, because top-p is the better rule anyway and there is no value to translate. These five are the ones that cost work. **Missing penalties on Anthropic is the one that bites**: a feature tuned with `frequency_penalty=0.5` to break loops has no equivalent, and the repetition has to be handled in the prompt instead.

d.title: Normalising the names while the behaviours differ is worse than not abstracting
d.caption: The instinct on meeting the support matrix is to build a layer that hides it, and that is usually the wrong shape — **the differences that matter are behaviours, not parameter names**. An abstraction that smooths the names is actively misleading, because it makes switching providers *look* like a configuration change, and the eval step then gets skipped on the strength of the abstraction's promise. Switching providers is a project.

nodes.label: The support matrix looks like config
Treat it as a project instead

d.title: The text alone distinguishes none of these
d.caption: A complete answer, a truncated one, a tool request and a blocked response can all arrive as a short string, and `finish_reason` is the only field that tells them apart. Which is why reading it is not optional: code that branches on the content and ignores this field is guessing, and it guesses wrong precisely in the cases that matter — a JSON response cut at `max_tokens` is unparseable, and a prose answer cut there merely looks brief.

d.title: One of these can prevent a 429; the other only explains it
d.caption: They look like the same kind of telemetry and they are not. **`usage` is an audit record** — it arrives after the work is done, so it cannot prevent anything, but it is what reconciles your cost model against the invoice. **The rate-limit headers are a control signal** — they arrive on every response and say how much headroom is left, which is enough to slow down *before* a 429 rather than back off after one.

d.title: What is worth retrying, and what retrying only costs you
d.caption: The dividing line is whether the same request could plausibly succeed. A 429 or a 5xx is transient, so backoff is exactly the right tool — and honour `retry-after` when it is present rather than guessing. The 'no' rows are deterministic: a malformed request will be malformed again, a blocked input will be blocked again, and an over-long prompt needs fixing rather than resending. **A timeout is the hard one**, because the request may already have been processed.
